criteria.note: Ball valves with red handles and brass fittings with water meters are visible in the open floor hatch.
Two red-and-grey lever handles are clearly visible on the grey pipes.
The hatch is dark and shows no clear drips, but the lower areas are too shadowed to judge fully.

rows.retakeHint: Retake with a torch or light on the pipes, close to the valves, so the fittings and floor of the hatch are well lit.
rows.note: Flat's tiled access hatch: two red-lever ball valves, filters and water meters, no visible leak or stains. Lever position must not be judged.

criteria.note: A blue ball valve body is partly visible below the water meter, though the meter dominates the frame.
A blue lever handle is visible at the bottom of the frame, partly cropped.
Valve is only partly in frame, so leaks or corrosion at it cannot be judged reliably.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the whole shut-off valve, with its handle and pipe connections, in good light.
rows.note: Outdoor meter with a blue-lever ball valve below; the valve is partly cut off at the bottom edge, so a retake is defensible.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter's display and label, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at a valve cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve with its handle, usually on the pipe next to the water meter.
rows.note: Electronic water meter lying on a table, not installed; no shut-off valve in frame.

criteria.note: Several shut-off valves are visible on an outdoor pipe manifold with water meters, though which one serves the flat is unclear.
A small handle is visible on the valve beside the top-left meter, and others are partly visible.
Black-and-white photo with plants partly covering the pipes, so leaks, stains or corrosion at the valves can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take a colour close-up of the valve you use to shut off the flat's water, with plants moved aside and good light.
rows.note: Black-and-white outdoor wall with several meters and small valves of a shared building; which valve is the home's is unclear and corrosion can't be judged in B/W. Corroded pipework makes fix_first defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: The photo shows a water meter dial, not a shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever is visible, only the meter face.
No valve is in frame, so leaks at a valve can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the shut-off valve with its handle, usually on the pipe next to the water meter.
rows.note: Close-up of a dirty meter dial, no valve in frame (sample photo).

criteria.note: This is an outdoor excavated water meter box with pipework, not a flat's own or appliance shut-off valve.
No valve handle or lever can be identified in the photo.
No valve is clearly visible, so leaks or corrosion at a valve can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the shut-off valve inside your flat (e.g. under the sink or near the water entry), with the handle in frame and close enough to see.
rows.note: Street excavation with the utility's meter box, lid closed, no lever visible; wrong subject (the valve is inside the building).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve body is clearly visible on the pipe.
A metal lever with a green grip is visible beside the valve.
No drips, water stains or corrosion are visible; only minor solder marks on the copper joints.

rows.note: Brass ball valve with a green lever on copper pipe, clean (sample photo).

criteria.note: A brass ball valve sits between copper pipes and is clearly in frame.
A dark lever handle with a metal bracket is visible below the valve.
No drips or water seen, but slight greenish tint at the left joint could be corrosion.

rows.retakeHint: Take a well-lit close-up of the valve and its joints so any green or white deposits can be judged.
rows.note: Brass ball valve on copper pipe with a black lever; the lever position is ambiguous but never judged.

criteria.note: Only a close-up of a braided hose section is shown; neither the valve nor the machine end is visible.
No shut-off valve is visible in the frame.
Braided hose looks intact here, but connections are not visible and most of the hose is blurred.

rows.retakeHint: Step back and photograph the whole hose, including the wall valve and the connection to the machine, in focus.
rows.note: Macro of a braided steel hose only: neither the machine nor its tap is in frame.

criteria.note: A braided hose is shown close up, but its far end at the machine is cut off at the top right.
Only part of a valve fitting is visible at the bottom edge, and it is cut off and out of focus.
The focused part of the hose looks undamaged, but the connections are blurred or cut off, so the full hose can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Step back so the whole hose, from the wall valve to the machine, and the valve are in frame and in focus.
rows.note: Braided hose into a chrome angle valve, shallow focus; no machine in frame, so the hose is not visible from tap to machine.

criteria.note: A white P-trap under a sink is clearly visible.
Water is dripping from the bottom of the trap.

rows.fix: Clean the drain or trap: lift off the cover, remove hair and dirt, and rinse. If a nut leaks, tighten it.
rows.note: White plastic sink trap with water dripping from it: leak at the trap, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: Photo shows a loose brass valve part with threaded fittings held up, not an installed dishwasher connection.
Only a detached valve component is shown, not an installed shut-off valve for a dishwasher.
No installed hose or connection is visible, so leaks can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed dishwasher hose and shut-off valve under the sink, with the whole connection in frame.
rows.note: A hand holding a loose brass valve with thread tape: a loose part, not an installed connection. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: White waste pipe assembly with compression nuts and a short bottom outlet is visible under the sink.
No drips, water, stains or leaks are visible on the pipes, joints or cabinet floor.

rows.note: Open under-sink cupboard: plastic trap with an appliance branch, dry clean floor, no leak. (No drip tray, but that is L4, not L5.)

criteria.note: Only a small white pipe section is visible at the top; the trap is hidden by someone in the cabinet.
The trap area is blocked from view, so leaks or blockage can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take the photo with nothing blocking the view, showing the whole sink trap and pipes under the sink.
rows.note: A person lying in an open sink cupboard (legs only); the trap is not clearly visible. Never describe the person.

criteria.note: Only the sink strainers are visible; the trap is behind closed cabinet doors and no floor drain is in frame.
No standing water at the sink strainers, but the trap and any floor drain can't be seen.

rows.retakeHint: Open the cabinet under the sink and photograph the trap and pipes below the sink, with good lighting.
rows.note: Kitchen with the lower cupboard doors closed; the trap is not visible (sample photo).

criteria.note: This shows a braided hose on a white ceramic fixture, not a dishwasher connection.
An angle valve is visible, but it is not shown serving a dishwasher.
No drips or stains are visible, but the dishwasher connection is not shown, so it can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the space under the kitchen counter showing the dishwasher's hose, its connection and the shut-off valve.
rows.note: Toilet supply: braided hose and angle stop valve under a toilet cistern; wrong appliance for the dishwasher check.

criteria.note: A distribution board with rows of circuit breakers and blanking covers fills the frame.
No scorch marks, damage, missing covers or exposed live parts are visible; gaps are filled with blanking covers.
Several RCD units with TEST buttons are visible, including an ABB F204 on the lower right.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the board.

rows.note: Modern ABB board: RCDs with TEST buttons, B16 breakers, labelled circuits, cover on (sample photo).

criteria.note: An old electricity meter board with fuse holders is visible in a recess.
Fuse covers are removed and lying nearby, leaving exposed wiring and fuse holders; dirty, aged board.
No RCD with a TEST button is visible on this board.
Tools, fuse covers and parts are lying in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old single-phase installation with porcelain screw-fuse holders, a removed fuse and tools on the floor: exposed parts, no RCD.

criteria.note: Two empty distribution board enclosures are shown, a cover and a base with DIN rail and terminal bars.
These look like new, uninstalled empty enclosures, so an installed board's condition can't be judged.
No RCD or breakers are fitted; the enclosures are empty.
Boards are unmounted and empty; a wrapped item lies on the cover, so installed clearance can't be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Photograph the installed, mounted fuse box with its cover on and the RCD with TEST button in view.
rows.note: An empty consumer-unit enclosure with its cover beside it, bare DIN rail, no breakers: not an installed board. fix_first (missing cover, no RCD) is defensible. Never verified.

criteria.note: A distribution board with breakers and wiring is clearly in frame.
The cover is off and wiring, terminals and busbar are openly exposed.
RCBO units labelled RCBO1 and RCBO2 are visible with blue TEST buttons.
Nothing is stored in front of the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Consumer unit with its front cover removed: RCBOs and exposed terminals, urgent (sample photo).

criteria.note: A wall-mounted breaker panel with its door open is fully in frame.
The inner cover is in place, with no scorch marks, damage or exposed live parts visible.
Two breakers at positions 6 and 12 show yellow TEST buttons.
Nothing is stored in front of or against the panel.

rows.note: US breaker panel, door open, dead front on, handwritten circuit numbers, two GFCI breakers with TEST buttons (residual-current protection).

criteria.note: Only a single isolated RCD device is shown on a white background, not a fuse box or distribution board.

No board is shown, so the area in front of it cannot be judged.

rows.retakeHint: Take a photo of your actual fuse box or distribution board in your home, with the cover open and the whole board in frame.
rows.note: Product photo of an ABB RCD on a white background: not the home's board.

Heavy rust, worn paint and grime on the panel and enclosures; some cables hang loosely and a plug dangles.
No modern RCD with a TEST button can be seen on the board.
A loose cable loop with a red plug hangs over a box on the board.

rows.fix: Clear the space in front of the fuse box. If you see damage or scorch marks, or there is no RCD, call an authorised electrician. Do not fix it yourself.
rows.note: Old industrial cast-metal switchgear (ASEA) with covers on but no RCD visible. A retake (not a home board) is defensible. Never verified.
